newsitem.title: FRANCE: French political leaders target undecided voters.
newsitem.headline: French political leaders target undecided voters.

text.p: French politicians reached out to undecided voters on Monday, just a week before the first-round of a hotly contested parliamentary election.
"More than a third of voters have not made up their minds," Jean-Marie Le Pen of the extreme-right National Front told France Inter radio. "I am convinced we will see a beautiful surprise on Sunday."
Pollsters predict the Front will win at most three seats and could end up with none at all in the National Assembly, where it now has none.
But Le Pen -- and others -- were hoping for an upset.
No more polls will be published before the conclusion of the May 25-June 1 election under an official ban which took effect at midnight on Saturday.

The final polls made public before the ban showed the governing centre-right in the lead but a leftist alliance of France's Socialists, Communists and ecologists gaining ground and within reach of an upset victory.
The polls also found a third or more of voters saying they might change their minds before Sunday's first round.
"I have the feeling we are getting what marathon runners call a second wind, which will carry us to victory," Socialist Julien Dray said.
"I believe victory is possible -- not certain but possible," he told Radio J.

Gaullist former prime minister Edouard Balladur appealed to free-market conservatives meanwhile with proposals for more tax cuts and the elimination of 10,000 public-sector jobs a year for annual savings to the state of 10 billion francs ($1.7 billion).
"I would would like us to go as far as possible down this path (of cutting state costs)," Balladur said in an interview with Le Monde.
"Our country has not yet taken account of all of the ramifications of globalisation and international competition. Fewer and fewer sectors will be sheltered," he said.
Socialist former prime minister Laurent Fabius, in a second Le Monde interview, said voters would have to choose on Sunday between the left's "humanism" and the right's "financially driven" policies.
The choice came down to "major changes...driven solely by financial logic" versus policies that "take human beings into account," he said.

Gaullist candidate Patrick Stefanini, a close ally of unpopular Prime Minister Alain Juppe, said it would be logical for Juppe to remain prime minister until the shift to a single European currency at the start of 1999.
"There would be a certain logic for him to remain prime minister until this matter is wrapped up," Stefanini told Radio J.

To Socialist and Gaullist critics alike, Juppe has come to personify the centre-right coalition's election woes. The Socialists attack his programmes while majority deputies accuse him of lacklustre leadership of the government's campaign.
But Gaullist President Jacques Chirac has given no hint he intends to replace him should the centre-right hold on to power.
A close aide to Chirac, meanwhile, said the president was weighing a second intervention in the campaign but may wait until after the first round before addressing the nation.

Francois Baroin, a Chirac speech-writer and political adviser, told Europe 1 radio the president would make up his mind after returning early on Monday from a state visit to China and a stopover in Moscow.
Jospin has said he would demand a right of reply if Chirac broadcasted to the nation just before the first round of voting.
